source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling
finding: Key paper. Authors sweep reasoning budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens in 500-token steps with budget forcing (append Wait, force end-of-thinking). They define marginal utility MU(t)=Acc(t+500)-Acc(t) and track per-problem answer changes (flip events). Gains shrink with budget and turn negative.
numbers: Models: DeepSeek-R1-32B and s1-32B. Data: AIME 2024+2025 (60 problems), MATH-500 by level, GPQA Diamond (198). Temperature 0. At 500 tokens baseline accuracy 28.2% (R1), 24.8% (s1). Early gain about +3.2 points per 500 tokens for R1; MU turns negative beyond about 12K tokens; R1 accuracy drop 12K to 16K is -0.9 points, 95% CI [-1.4,-0.4].
limits: Two open 32B models, math and one science set, greedy decoding, no proprietary models. Budget forcing may itself cause artifacts (authors test this, see a05). Table 1 text is partly garbled in the PDF extract, so MU per range is read from prose only.
agent_relevance: Gains from more tokens fade; a hard cap near the peak costs almost nothing in accuracy. Extended reasoning is associated with abandoning previously correct answers.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling (flip events)
finding: Flip events: a correct-to-wrong change between budgets is a negative flip, wrong-to-correct is positive. The negative to positive flip ratio rises above 1 at about 7K tokens for R1 (about 5K for s1).
numbers: R1-32B on AIME, cumulative flips from each budget onward, ratio: 0.71 (5K), 0.87 (6K), 1.09 (7K), 1.42 (8K), 3.29 (12K), 7.55 (16K). Bootstrap 1,000 samples: 8K CI [1.21,1.68] p=0.014; 12K CI [2.87,3.82]; 16K CI [6.12,9.24] p<0.001; 7K reported as p=0.038 in text but with a table CI of [1.01,1.18]; 6K CI [0.71,1.05] still includes 1.
limits: Ratios are cumulative counts over transitions, so one problem can count many times. Flip ratio and MU agree in sign but flip ratio crosses first (Spearman 0.89).
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable trigger: when wrong-to-right changes stop being the majority, stop thinking.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling (difficulty)
finding: The point where more thinking starts to hurt depends on problem difficulty. Easy problems peak early; hard ones peak late.
numbers: MATH-500 optimal budget by level, read from figure labels: about 1.0K (L1), 3.0K (L2), 4.5K (L3), 5.0K (L4), 7.5K (L5) tokens. Text: easy problems cross the overthinking line near 2K tokens versus 8K for hard.
limits: Difficulty comes from MATH level labels, which are not model-specific. Figure values are approximate.
agent_relevance: Supports G12: allocate thinking per problem difficulty, not uniformly.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling (qualitative and indicators)
finding: Hand check of 80 negative flips: most are real second-guessing. Cheap trace signals predict negative flips.
numbers: 80 sampled negative flips from R1 on AIME: 54 (67.5%) genuine overthinking (model explicitly rejects a correct answer), 16 (20.0%) exploration divergence (new valid method, arithmetic slip), 10 (12.5%) degradation (repetition). Indicators: answer oscillation r=0.78 with negative flips; all indicators combined r=0.82, 76.3% precision at 80% recall.
limits: Manual coding by the authors, single model. Indicators were evaluated on the same AIME set used for stopping, so results may be optimistic.
agent_relevance: An oscillation count (answer changed 2+ times) is a code-checkable stop or impasse signal that needs no model judgment.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling (natural vs forced; GPQA)
finding: Overthinking also shows without budget forcing and on science questions.
numbers: 312 natural R1 samples over 8K tokens: flip ratio above 10K tokens 1.31 natural vs 1.42 forced. GPQA Diamond R1-32B: accuracy peaks 55.6% at 10K, 54.9% at 12K, 53.1% at 16K; flip ratio 0.51 (4K), 0.93 (8K), 1.18 (10K), 2.84 (16K).
limits: Natural samples are selected by being long, which confounds with hard or confused problems. GPQA decline is only about 2.5 points from peak.
agent_relevance: Effect is modest on science; the case for a cap rests on cost savings more than on accuracy gains.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling (cost-aware early stopping)
finding: A cost-aware utility with parameter lambda shows optimal budgets shifting down as cost matters. Indicator-based early stopping keeps most accuracy.
numbers: lambda=0.5: stopping at 6K gives 50% compute cut with about 6 points accuracy loss. lambda=1.0 favors 2K. Combined-indicator early stopping reaches 97% of peak accuracy with 60% of the compute (AIME).
limits: Compared with fixed caps on the same data used to tune the indicators; no held-out test is reported.
agent_relevance: Pay-for-itself test (G7): report accuracy against tokens, not accuracy alone.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR)
finding: Builds tasks where longer reasoning lowers accuracy. Four families: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, deduction (zebra puzzles), and AI-risk questions. Five failure modes: Claude gets distracted, o-series overfit to framing, drift to spurious features, loss of focus on deduction, more self-preservation talk in Claude Sonnet 4.
numbers: Nine models tested. Three setups: controlled (prompt keywords dont think/think/think harder/ultrathink plus budgets 0 to 16,384 tokens; 3 repeats), natural (5 samples per question ranked by length), cautioned. Temperature 1.0 (Claude, OpenAI), 0.6 (open weights). Inverse scaling needs over 2% accuracy change or over 0.05 RMSE with non-overlapping CIs.
limits: Tasks were built by the authors to expose failure, so they say little about typical rates. Trends are often mixed or noisy across models.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G11: extra thinking can hurt when problems carry distractors or false framing.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR) (Misleading Math)
finding: Counting question with irrelevant numbers or famous-puzzle framing (Birthday Paradox style). Models with longer reasoning get pulled into the distractor.
numbers: Claude Opus 4: accuracy falls from near 100% to about 85-90% as reasoning lengthens (about 80% in the famous-paradox variant). DeepSeek R1 natural setup: 70% to 30% with five distractors. o3 stable in controlled setup, weak decline in natural. All models near-perfect on standard arithmetic benchmarks.
limits: Question difficulty is constant while distractors rise, so framing, not hardness, hurts. o3 uses shorter traces here, so length and model are confounded.
agent_relevance: Strip irrelevant context before long reasoning (S1 restate); do not trust longer traces on tricky-looking trivial items.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR) (regression, zebra, safety)
finding: Grades Regression: longer thinking moves predictions toward less predictive features. Zebra puzzles decline in the natural setup. The survival-instinct item shows model-specific drift.
numbers: Grades Regression zero-shot: Sonnet 3.7, Opus 4, o3-mini show inverse scaling in controlled setup; Qwen3-32B shows positive scaling; others noisy or flat. Natural setup mostly noisy. Survival Instinct: Claude Sonnet 4 willingness to be turned off 60% to 47%; o3 72% to 76%; R1 stable 71-72%. Few-shot examples reduce but do not remove the effect.
limits: Most safety tasks showed weak or noisy trends; Survival Instinct was chosen after seeing clear patterns (selection effect). Mixed results are reported openly.
agent_relevance: Evidence is mixed: inverse scaling is task- and model-specific, not universal. Run an own check before relying on a cap.

source: Chen et al. (2024) On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs (Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=?)
finding: First named study of overthinking in o1-like models: too many tokens for easy problems with no accuracy gain. Defines outcome efficiency (share of tokens used up to the first correct answer) and process efficiency (share of tokens in distinct strategies).
numbers: For 'what is 2 plus 3', o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. One example: 13 solutions, 7 distinct strategies, process efficiency 35.8%. Models: QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1-Preview; tested on ASDIV, GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME.
limits: Efficiency is defined on tokens, not on accuracy loss: overthinking here costs money but is not shown to add errors. Early models (Dec 2024).
agent_relevance: The waste is mostly later re-solving after a correct first answer, so stop-after-first-verified-answer is a cheap rule.

source: Chen et al. (2024) On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs (Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=?) (first-correct analysis)
finding: The first round of solutions is usually already correct; later rounds add little accuracy and little diversity. Simpler problems waste more.
numbers: In more than 92% of cases where the answer is correct the first solution round is correct; the first round is under 60% of tokens (QwQ on ASDIV: 287 tokens, 38.7% of response). On MATH500 Level 1 outcome efficiency is under 50%.
limits: Counts only cases where the final answer was correct, so it cannot show later rounds that fixed a wrong first round.
agent_relevance: Supports G11: short first attempt plus independent checks beats one long chain on easy items.

source: Chen et al. (2024) On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs (Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=?) (mitigation)
finding: Self-training with SimPO on simplified responses cuts tokens while keeping accuracy. First-correct-solution only loses accuracy on hard sets; adding one reflection round fixes part of it.
numbers: SimPO cut generated tokens by 22.3% on MATH500 (best of the preference methods tested). FCS+Reflection beats plain FCS by 1.4% on MATH500. GPQA and AIME performance maintained with fewer tokens (table values not extracted cleanly).
limits: Training-based fix, not a scaffold fix. Hard problems still need long chains.
agent_relevance: Hard items need more reflection: caps must scale with difficulty (G12).

source: Wu et al. (2025) When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
finding: Accuracy follows an inverted U against number of CoT steps. Simple model: accuracy A(N) is proportional to ((1-E(N,M,T))(1-epsilon(T)))^N, so each added step adds a chance of error while making steps easier. Optimal length N* rises with task difficulty T and falls with model capability M (a simplicity bias).
numbers: Real models (Qwen2.5 series, 30 questions each): optimal length falls from 14 steps (1.5B) to 4 steps (72B). Harder tasks need longer optimal CoT (positive correlation, p<=0.05, 100 questions, 60 samples each). Synthetic GPT-2: RL with PPO drifts to optimal N=5 at 96% accuracy. Length-filtered vote beats plain majority vote.
limits: Model is for arithmetic with clean step structure; reflection and backtracking are treated only as decomposition. Real-model optimum read from small question samples.
agent_relevance: Formal reason a cap should shrink as the base model gets stronger. Re-check the cap on each model version.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Extending thinking with Wait or Think more first helps, then hurts. Their probabilistic model says extra thinking raises output variance, which looks like improvement at first but then lowers precision. Parallel thinking at the same token budget with majority vote works better.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill models (1.5B, 7B, 8B), GSM-8K, MATH-500, AIME 2024. First panel: accuracy 82.2% to 87.3% as thinking grows 385 to 1,100 tokens, then falls to 70.3% at 15,980 tokens. Exact-token setup shows a decline throughout. Parallel thinking: up to 22% (intro) or 20% (abstract) higher accuracy at 16K tokens.
limits: Abstract and intro disagree (20 vs 22). Variance account is a toy 1-D model, not a proof for real transformers. Wait-appending is not natural reasoning.
agent_relevance: Supports G4/G11: several short independent attempts and code voting beat one long chain at equal tokens.

source: Cuadron et al. (2025) The Danger of Overthinking: Examining the Reasoning-Action Dilemma in Agentic Tasks
finding: In agent tasks (SWE-bench Verified, CodeAct in OpenHands), overthinking means preferring internal simulation to acting on environment feedback. An LLM judge scores 3,908 trajectories on analysis paralysis, rogue actions and premature disengagement. Higher score goes with lower issue resolution.
numbers: Reasoning models score nearly 3 times higher on overthinking than non-reasoning models. Choosing the lower-overthinking of 2 low-effort o1 runs: 27.3% resolved at $800 vs 29.1% for high effort at $1,400 (43% cheaper); with 3 samples 30.3% vs 29.1%. o1-low had 35% higher overthinking score than o1-high.
limits: Correlational. Judge is Claude Sonnet 3.5 with no outcome access, validated against human raters. This definition differs from token waste: here MORE reasoning tokens went with LESS overthinking in o1.
agent_relevance: A different failure: over-reasoning instead of acting. For tool use, check real output (G2) rather than keep simulating.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Puzzles with controllable size (Tower of Hanoi, Checker Jumping, River Crossing, Blocks World). Three regimes: at low complexity non-thinking models match or beat thinking models; at medium thinking helps; at high both collapse to zero. Trace position analysis shows overthinking at low complexity.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini; 64k max tokens. Tower of Hanoi N=1-4: accuracy of intermediate solutions falls or oscillates as thinking proceeds; N=5-7 slightly rises; N>=8 near zero. Correct solution found early, then wrong alternatives explored. Hanoi N=5 (31 moves) near perfect but River Crossing fails at N=3 (11 moves).
limits: Disputed (see a17). Critics claim output limits and puzzle design issues.
agent_relevance: Low-complexity regime supports S0: easy items go to the plain model.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (comment on Shojaee et al.)
finding: Challenge to the collapse claim: output token limits, scoring that cannot tell inability from refusal to list every move, and unsolvable River Crossing instances for N>=6. When asked for a generating function instead of the full move list, models do well on Hanoi sizes reported as failed.
numbers: Cites a social media replication showing models writing 'to avoid making this too long, I'll stop here'. Preliminary only, no table of numbers.
limits: Informal, short comment; preliminary experiments. Does not address overthinking at low complexity, only the collapse at high complexity.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: judge reasoning limits against budget and format, not only accuracy. Collapse is partly a harness effect.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
finding: Uses psychology of verbal overshadowing and deliberation costs to predict where CoT hurts. In three task types CoT lowers accuracy: implicit statistical learning, visual stimuli hard to verbalise, and learning labels with exceptions.
numbers: Artificial grammar learning (440-problem subset): GPT-4o 94.0% direct vs o1-preview 57.7%, a 36.3 point drop; GPT-4o with CoT 87.5% to 64.4% (-23.1); Claude 3 Opus -8.0; Gemini 1.5 Pro -6.05; Llama 3.1 70B -8.8; Claude 3.5 Sonnet -1.8 (p=0.969, no effect). Exceptions task: up to 331% more trials to learn labels (GPT-4o 2.9 to 12.5).
limits: Three other task types gave mixed or no CoT harm because models differ from humans (long context, existing logic priors). Not a model-by-model replication of human findings.
agent_relevance: Psychology gives a prior: tasks that rely on intuition or pattern feel rather than stepwise rules are where to skip long thinking.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own tests of 20 datasets on 14 models. CoT gives large gains only on math and symbolic or logic tasks. On MMLU, CoT adds almost nothing unless the question or answer contains an equals sign.
numbers: Average CoT improvement: symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logical 6.9 points; average on these top three was 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. Nearly half the significant comparisons are MMLU and MMLU-Pro.
limits: About prompt CoT, not trained reasoning models. Shows low or zero benefit on non-symbolic tasks rather than harm.
agent_relevance: Gate S0: skip long reasoning when the task is not symbolic or multi-step.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking
finding: Skipping the thinking block (NoThinking) with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen matches or beats Thinking at equal tokens on seven datasets, mostly at low budget. NoThinking with N parallel samples is competitive with much slower Thinking.
numbers: At about 700 tokens on AMC 2023: NoThinking 51.3 vs Thinking 28.9. Parallel NoThinking comparable to Thinking with up to 9x longer latency. NoThinking pass@k gets close to Thinking as k grows.
limits: Distilled models; math, code and theorem proving. Advantage is at low budget and shrinks at large budgets.
agent_relevance: Plain answers plus voting is a strong baseline for the schema (G7, G11).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think
finding: RL trains the model to choose Thinking or NoThinking per problem, using NoThinking whenever accuracy holds. Shows NoThinking is better for relatively simple items in both accuracy and cost.
numbers: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: average response length down 53% and accuracy up 2.4% across tested math sets (abstract and intro).
limits: Training method, not a prompt or scaffold. Needs retraining per model.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as G12 learned by a model; our scaffold gets the gate from code-run difficulty signals.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Opposite failure: models switch between thoughts without finishing promising lines. Incorrect answers carry more switches and more tokens. A decoding penalty on switching tokens (TIP) improves accuracy.
numbers: o1-like models use 225% more tokens in incorrect than correct responses, with 418% more thought switches. Conventional LLMs show no such length difference. Models QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1-Preview, R1-671B on MATH500, GPQA, AIME.
limits: Observational; wrong answers are longer partly because hard problems are both longer and wrong. Complements overthinking: too many ideas, too little depth per idea.
agent_relevance: Two failures coexist: waste on easy items and shallow switching on hard ones. Cap per difficulty and detect switching.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: append Wait to extend thinking, or cut it. It lifts AIME24 but the gain flattens, and suppressing the stop token too often causes loops. This is the method the key paper uses.
numbers: AIME24 50.0 to 53.3 with 2x Wait (2x without string 50.0; 'Alternatively' 50.0; 'Hmm' 50.0), up to 57% at the largest budget. MATH500 93.0 falls to 90.2 with 2x and no string. Gains flatten at about six forced extensions. Intro claims s1-32B beats o1-preview by up to 27% on MATH and AIME24.
limits: 30 AIME questions, small n. Shows the rise before the fall that Zhou et al. measure further out.
agent_relevance: Wait-style prompts are not free; use them only with a check on the extended answer.

source: Sui et al. (2025) Stop Overthinking: A Survey on Efficient Reasoning for Large Language Models
finding: Survey defining overthinking: reasoning models make unnecessarily long traces, often finding the answer early, then continuing. Sorts fixes into model-based (RL length reward, SFT on short CoT), output-based (latent or compressed reasoning) and prompt-based (length hints, routing) methods.
numbers: Example: 'Which is larger, 0.9 or 0.11?' takes 602 words and 42 s for DeepSeek-R1. The survey cites 4,018 agent trajectories for Cuadron et al.; the source paper says 3,908.
limits: A review. The count mismatch shows secondary citation errors.
agent_relevance: Good map of mitigations; the prompt and routing family is what a scaffold can use without training.

source: Jurayj et al. (2025) Is That Your Final Answer? Test-Time Scaling Improves Selective Question Answering
finding: More compute raises correct answers and confidence in correct answers; adds confidence thresholds so models may abstain. Higher budgets sometimes lower accuracy among answered questions because more questions get answered (figure 1 caption).
numbers: Model DeepSeek R1-32B; no exact table read.
limits: Only abstract and first-page figure text were read; numbers not captured.
agent_relevance: Cited by Zhou et al. as the selective-prediction ancestor; relevant to G6 (abstain rule).
